# Spatial Pattern of Summer Bat Mortality from Collisions with Wind Turbines in Mixed-grass Prairie

## MARTIN D. PIORKOWSKI[1]

Department of Zoology, Oklahoma State University, 430 Life Sciences West, Stillwater 74078

## AND

## TIMOTHY J. O’CONNELL[2]

Department of Natural Resource Ecology & Management, Oklahoma State University, 240 Agricultural Hall, Stillwater 74078

ABSTRACT.—Spatial analysis that aims to identify site-specific hotspots of collision mortality from birds or bats striking wind turbines can potentially lead to mitigating measures that reduce mortality rates. During May–Jul. 2004 and 2005, we studied bird and bat mortality from collisions with wind turbines at a 102 megawatt, 68-turbine wind farm in the southern Great Plains, Oklahoma, USA. Standardized searches around turbine bases yielded 122 total carcasses of which 92 (75%) were found within 20 m of the turbine bases. We identified 111 carcasses of seven species of bats and 11 carcasses of 6 species of birds. Brazilian free-tailed bats (Tadarida brasiliensis) comprised 85% of bat carcasses collected. We corrected turbine collision estimates using searcher efficiency trials and a range of removal (i.e., ‘‘scavenging’’) rates reported in the literature. Estimated bat turbine collisions ranged from 1.19–1.71 fatalities/turbine (1.03–1.37/megawatt). These data provide some of the first evidence for a steady rate of collision mortality of Brazilian free-tailed bats at a North American wind farm, most likely due to the site’s proximity (,15 km) to a maternity colony. Spatial analyses indicated no consistent pattern in mortality estimates relative to ground cover or topographic position; but collision mortality was higher at several individual turbines, all of which were located near the heads of eroded ravines.

## INTRODUCTION

As the number of wind turbines has increased across North America, the potential influence of wind energy development on collision mortality of birds (Osborn et al., 2000; Johnson et al., 2002) and bats (Arnett et al., 2008) has received increasing study ( Johnson et al., 2003; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004). Bird mortality from collisions with anthropogenic structures has been well documented (see Coues, 1876; Cottam, 1929; Pulich, 1961; Avery, 1979; Klem, 1990; O’Connell, 2001; Erickson et al., 2001). Compared to these other causes of collision mortality, the number of birds killed by wind turbines is low (Erickson et al., 2001). For bats, reported rates of collision mortality with wind turbines vary in magnitude across the U.S. (Osborn et al., 1996; Erickson et al., 2003; Johnson et al., 2003, 2004; Williams, 2003; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; Kunz et al., 2007; Arnett et al., 2008) with the highest rates observed along forested ridges of the Appalachians (Williams, 2003; Fiedler, 2004; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; NWCC, 2004; Arnett et al., 2008).

To date, most published data on bat collisions with wind turbines address migratory species in passage (Erickson et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2003; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004),

especially solitary tree roosters such as silver-haired (Lasionycteris noctivagans), red (Lasiurus borealis) and hoary (L. cinereus) bats (Caire et al., 1989; Arnett et al., 2008; Baerwald and Barclay, 2009). Research suggests that most collision mortality occurs during late summer and early autumn migration ( Johnson et al., 2003; Fiedler, 2004; Arnett et al., 2005, 2008).

Contrasting the literature on collision mortality of migratory bats in passage, no study to date has specifically examined the influence of wind facilities near large maternity colonies such as those of Brazilian free-tailed bats (Tadarida brasiliensis) in which single colonies can number up to 20 million individuals (Harvey et al., 1999). Individuals from such colonies have been shown to forage as far as 68 km from their roost cave (Best and Geluso, 2003). We have little information on the degree to which mortality during late spring and early summer (when females make daily flights from their roosts over a period of many weeks) can influence the viability of a given roost location. From a management perspective, we also lack information on the spatial distribution of collision mortality, which could vary from one wind turbine to the next as a function of local topography, vegetation cover and/or specific flight corridors habitually used by bats leaving and returning to their roosts. The identification of individual wind turbines at which unusually high numbers of collisionkilled bats are found could provide support for the ‘‘coincidental collision hypothesis’’ (Cryan and Barclay, 2009) and lead to mitigating operational procedures for those turbines that could greatly reduce overall mortality rates reported for a site.

To increase our understanding of spatial pattern in bat mortality from collisions with wind turbines, we conducted May–Jul. carcass surveys for turbine-killed bats at a wind farm in western Oklahoma, USA. The Oklahoma Wind Energy Center (OWEC) is located approximately 15 km from two long-term aggregations of summering bats. One is a maternity colony comprised of approximately 1.5 million Brazilian free-tailed bats (Glass, 1982); the other is a mixed colony of male Brazilian free-tailed bats and cave myotis (Myotis velifer) totaling approximately 500,000 individuals ( John Gay, pers. comm).

We tested the hypothesis that collision mortality was randomly distributed among the 68 wind turbines at the Oklahoma Wind Energy Center. Our objectives were to (1) estimate a summer season, per-turbine rate of bat collision mortality and (2) analyze the spatial distribution of collisions at the OWEC relative to vegetation cover, topography and location of individual wind turbines.

## METHODS

From May through Jul. in 2004 and 2005, we studied summer collision mortality at the Oklahoma Wind Energy Center (OWEC) in northwestern Oklahoma, USA. The OWEC is a 68-turbine, 102-megawatt (MW) facility occupying approximately 472 ha in Harper and Woodward counties. Each turbine consists of a 100-m tubular metal tower on which is attached a variable speed and pitch rotor assembly with three 77-m blades. Individual turbines are mostly arranged in a linear pattern separated by 200–300 m from adjacent turbines.

## STUDY AREA

The OWEC is located in the central and southern mixed grasslands ecoregion (Ricketts et al., 1999) (Fig. 1, inset). Land use in the region is characterized by mixed rangeland [in which little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) forms the dominant grass cover] and small grain agriculture (primarily wheat). Approximately 43 of 68 wind turbines at the OWEC occur along the heads of seasonally dry riparian ravines that drain into the Cimarron River. Some of these ravines include crevasses communicating with gypsum caverns that create

FIG. 1.—Wind turbines at the Oklahoma Wind Energy Center, Oklahoma identified as ‘‘hot spots’’ of collision mortality for Brazilian free-tailed bats in 2004 and 2005 combined

conditions suitable for colonial bats. The ravines support wooded riparian vegetation typical of the region, dominated by eastern redcedar ( Juniperus virginianus), eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides), American elm (Ulmus americana) and hackberry (Celtis laevigata) (Tyrl et al., 2002). Due largely to decades of fire suppression in this region (Fuhlendorf and Smeins, 1997), redcedar from the ravines has invaded upland pastures over much of the OWEC area.

## SEARCH DESIGN

To obtain raw estimates of summer collision mortality, we visually inspected the base of all 68 turbines for bird and bat carcasses in 2004 and 2005. We conducted two surveys (late May and late Jun.) in 2004, and four surveys (about every 14 d 15 May–15 Jul.) in 2005. For each carcass, we recorded species, GPS location, habitat, elevation and in 2005, the distance from the base of the turbine. We photographed each carcass in place before collection and deposited fresh specimens in the Collection of Vertebrates (COV) at the Oklahoma State University.

We searched for carcasses by walking circular transects (Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004) around the base of each turbine at 5, 10 and 15 m from the base. This afforded the ability to detect carcasses within a standardized search area within 20 m of each turbine base (1.3 ha total search area/turbine). Our search pace was approximately 20–30 m/min ( Johnson et al., 2003; Arnett et al., 2005) with speed adjusted according to vegetation and terrain. Vegetation cover around the turbines was sparse in 2004 and 2005, providing excellent visibility of carcasses within the search area. Thus, we are confident that the rate at which we detected carcasses within 20 m was similar among all 68 turbines. We collected carcasses found at any distance from turbines; but, due to variability in vegetation cover and topography with increasing distance from turbine bases, we were not confident of a consistent detection rate beyond 20 m. To eliminate interobserver detection bias, a single observer (MDP) conducted all carcass surveys.

We estimated observer detection rate for bats in 2005 with blind field trials (n 5 28) conducted by an independent party using to-scale models of dead bats. We built models from black blotter paper (folded to simulate wings) to which we glued tufts of gray rabbit (Sylvilagus sp.) pelt. We cut the pelts to represent the approximate torso length (70–90 mm) and width (20–30 mm) of the free-tailed bats we found beneath the turbines. We placed models at random locations within 20 m of turbine bases and recorded the location with a GPS receiver. The observer then applied normal carcass search protocols, and we recorded the proportion of models found by the observer. We considered the total proportion found in 28 trials to be the observer detection rate. We applied this rate a posteriori to all searches conducted in 2004 and 2005.

## ANALYSIS

We calculated three estimates of collision mortality based on (1) raw carcass counts, (2) raw counts divided by observer detection rate (Pd) and (3) raw counts modified by observer detection rate and removal rate (Pr). In practice, removal rates are calculated as ‘‘remaining rates,’’ i.e., 1.00 – the proportion of total removed. Because we did not calculate a sitespecific removal rate, we applied a full range of removal rates to represent likely minimum and maximum levels of scavenger or other removal at the OWEC (see Arnett et al., 2005). Because many of our collected specimens were in an advanced state of decomposition when found, we used Pr 5 0.00 to represent the lowest likelihood of removal at the OWEC, and Pr 5 0.79, the highest value reported in Arnett et al. (2005). We calculated adjusted counts using the equation m 5 (C/Pd)/Pr, where m is the estimated collision mortality, C is the raw carcass count, Pd is the searcher efficiency and Pr is the probability of carcasses remaining after removal trials (Arnett et al., 2005). As a final modifier for our mortality estimate [(C/ Pd)/Pr]/Pa, we used the measured distances to the turbine bases in 2005 to determine the cumulative frequency of carcasses located within 20 m (our effective search radius around turbine bases). We converted all estimates from collision mortality per turbine to collisions per MW (Arnett et al., 2008); however, Sovacool (2009) suggests using fatalities per kilowatt

hour for comparison among any form of electricity production (e.g., wind, nuclear or fossilfuel).

We assessed the broad spatial distribution of collision mortality by plotting carcass location in GIS ArcView 3.3 (Ormsby et al., 1999; ESRI, 2002). We compared rates of collision mortality among locations characterized by cover type and topography within 200 m. We compared mortality rates among ‘‘prairie,’’ ‘‘crop’’ and ‘‘mixed’’ cover types (O’Connell and Piorkowski, 2006) and between ‘‘flat’’ and ‘‘ravine’’ topography. We analyzed mortality by habitat and topography by use of one-way ANOVA with Minitab Statistical Software (Minitab, 1995).

For analysis of fine-scale spatial distribution of collision mortality, we used ‘‘Hot Spot’’ analysis in ArcInfo/ArcGIS 9.2 (ESRI, 2008). The analysis consists of a null randomization model test of a sample distribution of spatial attributes. For each weighted point in a projection, the Hot Spot tool calculates a Getis-Ord Gi* statistic (interpreted as a Z-score with a 5 0.05) based on attribute similarity among the point and all neighboring points within 800 km (i.e., threshold distance). The Hot Spot test assumes a spatially random distribution (in Euclidean distance) of the proportional sum of the total attribute value (e.g., collision fatalities) for the entire sample. An unusually high proportion of the attribute sum located at a point or points results in high Z-scores for those points and is interpreted as a spatially significant phenomenon.

For our Hot Spot analysis, we used the total number of Brazilian free-tailed bat carcasses detected within 36 m of a turbine base (n 5 68) as the attribute for each point in the projection. We used a 36 m cutoff to accommodate the maximum precision error from the GPS units for both the turbine location and the carcass location (both were 68m resulting in a possible combined error of 616 m).

## RESULTS

During 340 individual searches from May–Jul. in 2004 and 2005, we found 11 turbinekilled birds of six species and 111 turbine-killed bats of seven species. The majority (n 5 94) of carcasses were Brazilian free-tailed bats (Tadarida brasiliensis). Examination of 64 (58%) relatively fresh intact bat carcasses indicated a female-biased sex ratio for the two most common species encountered (Table 1).

The raw carcass counts for all bat species yielded estimates of 0.53 fatalities/MW in 2004 and 0.56 fatalities/MW in 2005. The single observer detected 67% of model carcasses during searcher efficiency trials. Using this probability of detection (Pd 5 0.67), we estimated total bat collision fatalities for the 1.3-ha search area around each turbine to have been 81 individuals (0.79/MW) in 2004 and 85 (0.83/MW) in 2005. For Brazilian free-tailed bats, we estimated collision fatalities to have been 73 individuals (0.72/MW) in 2004 and 67 (0.66/ MW) in 2005. When we further adjusted these rates to account for published removal estimates (e.g., 0.00–0.79; Arnett et al., 2005), we derived a modified estimate of 81–103 individuals (0.79–1.01/MW) in 2004 and 85–108 (0.83–1.06/MW) in 2005. For Brazilian free-tailed bats, we estimated the removal-adjusted range of mortality to have been 73–92 individuals (0.72–0.90/MW) in 2004 and 67–85 individuals (0.66–0.83/MW) in 2005.

Including standardized searches and incidental findings, we detected carcasses up to 46 m of turbine bases (mean 5 17 6 10 m). Of the total number of carcasses we detected, 77% were located within the 20 m search radius (Pa 5 0.77). Because we did not obtain a reliable estimate of the number of carcasses found beyond 20 m, we cannot state with confidence that our standardized surveys allowed for detection of 77% of the total number of carcasses.

Mortality was widespread at the OWEC; we found carcasses at 46 turbines (68%). In 2004, Brazilian free-tailed bat collision mortality was positively associated with ravine topography (F1,66 5 5.34, P 5 0.024) and marginally so with mixed cedar and pasture habitat (F2,65 5 2.69, P 5 0.076). This broad spatial bias in collision mortality was not repeated in 2005 with respect to topography (F1,66 5 0.10, P 5 0.751) or habitat (F2,65 5 0.06, P 5 0.938). Brazilian free-tailed bat mortality was not associated with topography (F1,134 5 2.22, P 5 0.138) or habitat (F2,133 5 1.11, P 5 0.332) when both years were combined.

Using 2004 and 2005 data for Brazilian free-tailed bats, three turbines emerged as significant ‘‘hot spots’’ of collision mortality (Fig. 1, triangles). All three turbines were located near the head of a forested ravine cut by an intermittent tributary to the Cimarron River. The three hotspot turbines were ,5% of the turbines at the OWEC, but they accounted for 16% of the Brazilian free-tailed bat carcasses we collected in 2004 and 2005.

Of 111 bat specimens collected, we selected the most fresh on which to perform necropsies. We ultimately examined 17 individuals for signs of soft tissue trauma and cleaned the skeletons using dermestid beetle larvae (Hall and Russell, 1933). Visual inspection of cleaned skeletons indicated 14 (82%) with broken bones and 3 (18%) with no apparent skeletal injury. Of the 14 specimens with skeletal injury, it was not obvious whether or not visceral hemorrhaging potentially consistent with barotraumas was present (Baerwald et al., 2008). However, of the three specimens with no apparent skeletal injury there was no obvious visceral hemorrhaging observed.

## DISCUSSION

We documented seven species of bats among the casualties during the two summers. The identification of a turbine-killed cave myotis [a United States Species of Concern (USFWS, 1996)] may be the first recorded casualty of this species at a wind farm, as it does not appear in compilations by Kunz et al. (2007) or Arnett et al. (2008). Brazilian free-tailed bats

comprised 78% of all fatalities (n 5 122) and 85% of all bat fatalities (n 5 111). The only other study to report Brazilian free-tailed bats was at the High Wind Power Project located in Solano County, California, USA where they accounted for 48 of 279 (17%) documented bat fatalities (Kerlinger et al., 2006). Although this species has thus far infrequently been reported among casualties, we speculate that Brazilian free-tailed bats are at least as susceptible to collision mortality as other species, and will be more frequently listed among the casualties as additional monitoring from within its range comes to light.

We attribute the high mortality of Brazilian free-tailed bats to the two known colonies in the area. A ‘‘maternity’’ colony occurred approximately 15 km north and a ‘‘bachelor’’ colony 15 km northeast of the OWEC. Brazilian free-tailed bats account for nearly 1.5 million (Glass, 1982) of an estimated 2 million bats within these two caves with cave myotis the second most abundant ( John Gay, pers. comm.). Of the 51 Brazilian free-tailed bat specimens in suitable condition for skeletal preparation by the Oklahoma State COV, most (34) were gravid females. We observed gravid hoary bats as well (Table 1). The hoary and red bat carcasses (n 5 13 combined) we encountered throughout the surveys suggest that at least some were residents (Cryan, 2003), possibly roosting in the riparian cedar/cottonwood forest (Carter et al., 2003) or forest edge habitat (Menzel et al., 1998).

In 2004, turbines in ravine topography were responsible for a higher rate of bat collision mortality than those in areas of low topographic relief, and there was some evidence that turbines in mixed cedar/pasture habitats claimed more victims than those in cropland and prairie habitats. These patterns, however, were not repeated in 2005 or through the combination of both years. This may be a result of different habitat use patterns by bats in 2004 and 2005 based on factors that we did not measure, specifically precipitation, wind velocities and storm fronts (Arnett et al., 2005). A Mesonet weather station, located 17 km north of the OWEC, recorded 22.28 cm and 40.00 cm of precipitation during the sampling periods in 2004 and 2005, respectively. This allowed for more standing water and more vegetation growth in 2005, potentially resulting in higher insect abundance throughout the landscape (Janzen and Schoener, 1968). If foraging efficiency was similar among habitats in varied topography in 2005 but not in 2004, this could explain the pattern of collision mortality we observed in 2004, and lead to the hypothesis that collision mortality is higher among wooded ravines during dry growing seasons.

Our analysis indicated that a cluster of turbines in Woodward County (Fig. 1) emerged as a hot spot of collision mortality, leading us to reject the hypothesis of random collision mortality among the 68 turbines at the OWEC. Cryan and Barclay (2009) outlined potential proximate and ultimate causes of bat collision mortality, and offered numerous hypotheses and predictions from each. Because we conducted our study in an area known to support large concentrations of Brazilian free-tailed bats during summer, many of the predictions related to mortality of migrant bats in passage did not apply. The spatial clumping of mortality of this one species at three turbines in one small area of the wind farm, however, suggests that bats moving through that area were more susceptible to collision, or that the number of bats regularly moving through that area was greater than at other areas of the OWEC. We interpret this result as providing support for the ‘‘coincidental collision’’ hypothesis (Cryan and Barclay, 2009), which in this case would probably be best explained by a landscape feature (eroded ravine) somehow serving as a conduit for the daily movements of many bats from the nearby maternity colony. The identification of a hotspot does not rule out the ‘‘attraction hypothesis’’ (Cryan and Barclay, 2009), although the ability to provide a mechanism through which bats would have been more attracted to hotspot turbines relative to the others was beyond the scope of our study.

As wind energy development expands in the American Southwest, the potential population impacts of that development in proximity to high concentrations of individuals, such as at maternity colonies, will need to be assessed (Kunz et al., 2007). Individuals may travel along discrete flight paths in their daily commute to preferred foraging areas; turbines operated within these paths could be responsible for many casualties. For example, Everaert and Stienen (2007) demonstrated the increased vulnerability of nesting terns (Sterna) to collision with wind turbines that had been erected along daily foraging paths. Unlike birds, bats do not seem to display avoidance behaviors in response to such structures (e.g., Desholm et al., 2006). Disproportionate mortality of bats that elect to forage in and around the wind facility also could influence population trajectory. Thus, our ability to reduce collision mortality may rest largely on our understanding of what conditions make some turbines more deadly than others.

The challenge for future work involves establishing the predictability of hot spots between seasons and years, as well as identifying specific attributes of the hot spot that differ from other turbines. We do not know, for example, if wind speed or direction had an influence on collision mortality in the hot spot cluster. If additional monitoring at the OWEC continues to point to these turbines as hot spots for mortality, then mitigating management (e.g., curtailment of those specific units under specific conditions) could be developed. The degree to which any recommendations for curtailment can be pinpointed to individual turbines benefits power providers by ensuring that non-offending turbines may be operated with little concern for collision mortality. At the same time, directed curtailment of a small number of especially dangerous turbines could achieve a desired reduction in collision mortality that is compatible with a desired level of power generation.
